tutorialHtml:
DENIZ AKKABAK · TIME GLITCH TUTORIAL · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

MADE IN INVIDEO · invideo.io/i/DENIZ-ig

Pharaoh’s Day Off

A Time Glitch episode: one Pharaoh, one ordinary day, fourteen modern objects, all filmed in secret on a phone by people who were not supposed to be watching.

A TUTORIAL BY DENIZ AKKABAK · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

PIPELINE NANO BANANA 2.1 → SEEDANCE 2.5 · 16:9 · 14 SCENES · 1:57 · AUDIO ON · BUILT IN INVIDEO

The first Time Glitch episode worked because every scene looked like it had actually happened. This one took three rebuilds to get back there, and the lesson is worth more than any single prompt: realism is not about resolution or detail, it is about where the camera is. The first version put the camera right inside the action and everything looked like a film set. The version in this document puts the camera far away, behind a column, through a lattice, among the reeds, in the hands of someone who is not supposed to be filming.

The comedy follows the same rule as before: one modern object per scene, one real physical consequence, and nobody treats it as strange. The Pharaoh brushes his teeth, takes a meeting in a massage chair, loses a quad bike race to ostriches and plays golf at Giza. Below is the full method, every still and every prompt exactly as it was run inside invideo.

THE PIPELINE AT A GLANCE

  1. 01

    Still — Nano Banana 2.1

    One 16:9, 2K image per scene, written as a real iPhone photo shot secretly from a distance: 2x–3x telephoto softness, over-sharpening, sensor noise, Smart HDR, and something in the foreground blocking part of the view.

  2. 02

    Video — Seedance 2.5, audio on

    The still goes in as @Image 1, explicitly as a reference only, never as the first frame. Ten seconds, 1080p, one continuous handheld shot, ambient sound and effects, no music.

STEP 01 — SETTING UP IN INVIDEO

Two Models, One Rule

  1. 01

    Nano Banana 2.1

    Aspect ratio 16:9, resolution 2K, thinking medium. There is no separate negative field, so every prompt ends with an “Avoid:” line.

  2. 02

    Seedance 2.5 (reference to video)

    Attach the still so it becomes @Image 1. Duration 10 seconds, resolution 1080p, audio generation on.

  3. 03

    Timeline

    All clips on one invideo timeline; each take trimmed to the window where the moment reads cleanly, and anything illogical cut.

STEP 02 — THE METHOD

The Hidden Phone

Two decisions do almost all of the work. First, distance: every still and every video describes a person hiding or standing at the back, zooming in with the phone, so the subject stays small to medium in the frame and something out of focus covers part of the picture. That single change removes the cinematic look, because nothing is composed for the camera any more.

Second, the reference is never the first frame. Every video prompt says “@Image 1 = reference only, NOT the first frame” and lets the shot start earlier and further away: the camera creeps down the corridor, waits behind the palm before the sprinklers turn on, watches the dust plumes on the horizon before the cars arrive. The still supplies the world; Seedance supplies the moment leading up to it. Two physical rules were added after revisions: mirrors must reflect only what the person holding them can see, and the golf ball only travels forward, in the direction of the swing.

SCENE 01 — STILL → SEEDANCE 2.5

The Snooze Button

Dawn, a priest pointing at the sunrise, and a servant quietly pressing snooze on a cheap digital alarm clock. Filmed from the far end of a dark corridor, through a half-open door, it plays like something you were never supposed to see.

SCENE 03 — STILL → SEEDANCE 2.5

One Braid at a Time

Cleopatra discovers the hair straightener, one braid at a time, with dozens still to go. The mirror physics are written out explicitly so the reflection behaves like a real mirror.

STEP 03

Anatomy — Why These Prompts Work

  1. 01

    Distance

    “Seen from far down a dim corridor”, “from the back of the hall”, “from among tall papyrus reeds on the opposite bank”. The subject is small to medium in the frame, never a close-up. Distance is what makes it feel found rather than staged.

  2. 02

    Something in the way

    A door frame, a lattice, a column, palm fronds, a camel’s neck, heads in a crowd. An out-of-focus obstruction in the foreground is the clearest signal that the person filming is hiding.

  3. 03

    The real iPhone texture

    “iPhone 3x telephoto look with slight digital-zoom softness, crisp computational over-sharpening, visible sensor noise, Smart HDR”. Describing the phone’s actual processing beats any generic “realistic” wording.

  4. 04

    Reference, not first frame

    “@Image 1 = reference only, NOT the first frame … it starts further back and reaches the moment on its own.” The video earns its gag instead of opening on it.

  5. 05

    The operator’s struggle

    “Sudden jerky 2x–3x digital zooms in and out, autofocus hunting, reacting a beat late.” A camera that is trying and failing to keep up is the opposite of cinematic.

  6. 06

    Real time, real physics

    “True real-time speed, real gravity” plus slow motion in every negative list, and explicit physics where the model drifts: the mirror that only shows its back, the ball that only flies forward.

  7. 07

    Sound from where the phone is

    Close sounds are what is near the hiding person (leaves, wind, a gasp); the action is heard far away and muffled. And no music, ever, so the edit stays free.

THE RESULT

Output — Pharaoh’s Day Off

Check your own cut against three things. Is the camera far enough away that nothing feels composed? Is something in the way? Does every scene start before its moment? And does each modern object cause one real, physical consequence that nobody finds strange? If all four hold, the glitch is believable.

ONE PHARAOH · ONE DAY · ONE HIDDEN PHONE

The closer you get, the less they believe you.

Swap Egypt for Rome, the Vikings or the court of Versailles, and the skeleton carries any era: a still written as a secret iPhone photo from a distance, something blocking the view, a reference that is never the first frame, one modern object with one real consequence, and sound heard from where the phone is.
